docs.title: Exam 1 — GPIO, boolean bit-packing and a hardware interrupt on a 3×3 grid
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Build a complete "lights-out" puzzle on a 3×3 grid of LEDs and buttons on the Pico 2 W — every GPIO explicitly configured, the whole board packed into one bit-packed integer touched only with bitwise operators, a hand-written RNG seeded from the hardware ring oscillator, and a restart button served by a hardware interrupt that works from any game state, including mid-victory.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Signal GPIO Direction Pull Notes LED bits 0–8 (LED_BASE = 0) GP0–GP8 output none — gpio_disable_pulls() 1 GPIO per LED. Position = bit index, row-major: bit 8 = top-left … bit 0 = bottom-right, as seen from the front in the setup image. Grid button bits 0–8 (BTN_BASE = 9) GP9–GP17 input pull-up — gpio_pull_up() Same position mapping as the LEDs. Pull-up means a press reads 0 Restart button (RESTART_BTN) GP18 input pull-up Not part of the 3×3 grid. Served by a falling-edge hardware interrupt, not polled (R5)

19 GPIOs total, all initialized together with gpio_init_mask(led_mask | btn_mask) and then split into outputs/inputs with sio_hw->gpio_oe_set / gpio_oe_clr — every line gets an explicit direction and pull in setup_hardware(), nothing is left at the reset default (R1). Each LED has a current-limiting resistor in series, sized for 3.3 V logic.

Pico 2 W with the 3×3 LED grid, the 3×3 button grid, and the separate restart button.

Non-default: the only external library linked besides pico_stdlib is hardware_rosc, added on purpose so the code can read rosc_hw->randombit directly:

target_link_libraries(exam1
        pico_stdlib
        hardware_rosc
        )

R6 bans a library RNG, so the board seed can't come from anything like rand(). Instead, setup_hardware() samples the ring oscillator's randombit 32 times (one delay_cycles(100) apart) to build a 32-bit seed, then feeds that into a hand-written xorshift32 for every board draw afterwards — the ROSC is only ever used once, to seed the shift register, not on every random number.

Quick reference I sketched to check physical position against bit index while wiring

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired 9 LEDs (GP0–GP8, current-limiting resistors) and 9 grid buttons + 1 restart button (GP9–GP18, internal pull-ups) on the breadboard.
  2. Packed the 3×3 board into one volatile uint32_t board_state, and hand-derived the 9 plus-shaped TOGGLE_MASKS[] (one XOR mask per button, clipped at the edges).
  3. Wrote custom_xorshift32() and seeded it bit-by-bit from rosc_hw->randombit; generate_new_board() applies 15 random masks and rejects boards that come out already-solved or solvable in one move.
  4. Registered a falling-edge interrupt on the restart button (gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback) that regenerates the board and clears victory_state from restart_isr().
  5. Polled the 9 grid buttons each loop with a one-shot flag per button plus a fixed-cycle debounce (delay_cycles(300000)), and declared victory as soon as board_state == 0, blinking all 9 LEDs with gpio_togl while ignoring grid input.

docs.title: Demo — full game running
docs.text: Random board on power-up, a few moves showing the plus-shaped toggle (center, edge and corner), a mid-game restart via the interrupt button, and the win animation.

docs.title: G1 — Control the display
docs.text: Each LED is an independent output on GP0–GP8; update_display() clears the whole 9-bit mask with sio_hw->gpio_clr and re-sets it from board_state << LED_BASE in one write. Physical position matches the bit order in the sketch above — that mapping is what makes TOGGLE_MASKS[] correct in the first place.

docs.title: G2 — Read the nine buttons reliably
docs.text:
Each button is read straight off sio_hw->gpio_in, masked to its own bit — pull-up means "pressed" is a 0:

uint32_t btn_bit = 1u << (BTN_BASE + i);
bool is_pressed = ((sio_hw->gpio_in & btn_bit) == 0);

A btn_flags[9] array (one flag per button, not board state — R2 only applies to the board itself) makes each press register exactly once: the flag goes up after a debounce confirms the press, and only comes back down after a second debounce confirms release, so holding a button doesn't repeat the move and two buttons held at once don't interfere with each other.

docs.title: G3 — The plus-shaped toggle
docs.text:
This is where the wiring mistake below showed up first. TOGGLE_MASKS[i] is precomputed per position instead of chasing neighbors at runtime:

const uint32_t TOGGLE_MASKS[9] = {
    0x00B, 0x017, 0x026, 
    0x059, 0x0BA, 0x134,
    0x0C8, 0x1D0, 0x1A0,
};
// applying a move is one line:
board_state ^= TOGGLE_MASKS[i];

Corners flip 3 bits, edges flip 4, the center flips 5 — the mask itself is what clips the pattern at the border, so there's no boundary if anywhere in the move logic (R3).

docs.title: G4 — Random starting board
docs.text: generate_new_board() XORs 15 random masks onto an empty board, then checks the result isn't 0 and isn't equal to any single TOGGLE_MASKS[i] (a one-move win) before accepting it — every generated board is reachable from empty in at most 15 moves, which also proves it's always solvable in reverse. Two consecutive restarts land on different boards because each restart re-draws from custom_xorshift32(), which never resets — only the initial seed came from the ROSC.

docs.title: G5 — Restart by interrupt
docs.text:
void restart_isr(uint gpio, uint32_t events) {
    if ((gpio == RESTART_BTN) && (events & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL)) {
        generate_new_board();
        update_display();
        victory_state = false;
    }
    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}

Registered once in setup_hardware() with gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(RESTART_BTN, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true, &restart_isr). Because it writes board_state and victory_state directly instead of setting a flag for the main loop to notice later, a restart takes effect immediately no matter what the main loop was doing — including mid-victory-blink (G6/R8).

docs.title: G6 — Victory condition
docs.text: board_state == 0 is checked once per main-loop pass, right after the button-handling block, so victory is flagged the same loop iteration the last LED goes out — no extra press needed. Once victory_state is true, the loop's top if skips the whole button-reading block and just toggles all 9 LEDs with sio_hw->gpio_togl, so grid presses can't change the board anymore and the blink can't be mistaken for a normal board.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text: On the first wiring pass, the LED legs went into the wrong GPIO columns relative to the bit-position sketch above — physically closer to a mirrored layout than the row-major, top-left-is-bit-8 order the code assumes.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: • update_display() clears and re-sets the full 9-bit LED mask on every button press, even though only 3–5 bits actually change. The victory blink already uses sio_hw->gpio_togl on the full mask — could a press instead do sio_hw->gpio_togl = TOGGLE_MASKS[i] << LED_BASE and skip touching the bits that don't change?

docs.title: Session 3 — Register-Level vs SDK GPIO Timing
docs.text:
Goal (one sentence): Compare the execution time between register-level instructions and SDK instructions.

Prediction — written before running anything: Assuming the SDK instruction takes 2 cycles and the register-level instruction takes 1 cycle (for example), I expect the frequency of the SDK instructions to be half the frequency of the register-level instructions.

docs.text:
• Pin map: GP18 → LED output; scope CH1 probe on GP18
  • Photo of setup:
  • Non-default: nothing.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
SDK version:

gpio_init(LED);
gpio_set_dir(LED, GPIO_OUT);

while (true) {
    gpio_put(LED, 1);
    gpio_put(LED, 0);
}

Register-level version:

const uint32_t LED_MASK = 1u << LED;

gpio_init(LED);
sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = LED_MASK;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_set = LED_MASK;
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = LED_MASK;
}

docs.text: • Forgot to include sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = LED_MASK; in the register-level version the first time.

docs.title: Session 4 — GPIO Bit-Pattern Animations (4-bit LED Bus)
docs.text:
Goal (one sentence): Drive four LEDs as a 4-bit register-level GPIO bus and reproduce four classic bit-pattern animations (binary counter, bouncing light, fill/empty, fill from the outside inward).

Exercises taken from GPIO Control — Embedded Systems I (LIIE1214).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: GP10 → PIN_D, GP11 → PIN_C, GP12 → PIN_B, GP13 → PIN_A (4-bit bus, one LED + resistor per pin); pushbutton on the breadboard for reset.
  • Photo of setup:
  • Non-default: nothing — same breadboard/board as Session 3, LEDs added on GP10–GP13.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired four LEDs (each with a series resistor) to GP10–GP13 on the same breadboard used in Session 3.
  2. Reused the register-level configuration validated in Session 3 (gpio_init per pin + a single sio_hw->gpio_oe_set with a 4-bit mask) instead of the SDK calls.
  3. Wrote one small program per exercise, changing only the animation logic inside while (true).
  4. Recorded each animation on video as evidence (table below, per exercise).

Shared setup code (identical in all four exercises — only the loop body changes):

#define PIN_A 13
#define PIN_B 12
#define PIN_C 11
#define PIN_D 10

const uint32_t MASK =
    (1u << PIN_A) | (1u << PIN_B) | (1u << PIN_C) | (1u << PIN_D);

gpio_init(PIN_A);
gpio_init(PIN_B);
gpio_init(PIN_C);
gpio_init(PIN_D);

sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK;   // OE = Output Enable

docs.title: Exercise 1 — 4-bit binary counter
docs.text:
Use the four LEDs as a 4-bit binary number and count from 0 to 15 on repeat, one LED pattern per count. (Reflective question from the guide: does the CPU know whether you wrote the value in decimal, hexadecimal, or binary? No — by the time it reaches the register it's just 4 bits.)

int counter = 0;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    sio_hw->gpio_set = (counter << 10);
    sleep_ms(500);

    counter++;
    if (counter > 15) {
        counter = 0;
        sleep_ms(1000);
    }
}

docs.title: Exercise 2 — Bouncing light
docs.text:
Move the lit LED across the four positions and back: 0001 → 0010 → 0100 → 1000 → 0100 → 0010 → 0001, repeating.

int counter = 0;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u << (counter + 10));
    sleep_ms(500);

    counter++;
    if (counter > 3) {
        while (counter > 0) {
            counter--,
            sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
            sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u << (counter + 10));
            sleep_ms(500);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Exercise 3 — Fill and empty animation
docs.text:
Turn LEDs on one by one from right to left, then off again, using gpio_togl on a single moving bit.

int counter = 0;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_togl = (1u << (counter + 10));
    sleep_ms(500);

    counter++;
    if (counter > 3) {
        counter = 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Exercise 4 — Fill from the outside inward
docs.text:
Light the two outer LEDs (PIN_A and PIN_D) first, then the two inner ones (PIN_B and PIN_C), toggling both edges of the bus symmetrically each step.

int counter = 0;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_togl = (1u << (counter + 10));
    sio_hw->gpio_togl = (1u << (13 - counter));
    sleep_ms(500);

    counter++;
    if (counter > 1) {
        counter = 0;
    }
}

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text: • Exercise 2: the first version had counter--, (comma) instead of counter--; (semicolon) inside the reverse loop. It still compiled and ran correctly — the comma operator just chains the expression into the next line — but it was luck, not intent; a stray comma elsewhere could easily change behavior silently.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: • Check the correct use of the >> shift operator instead of <<.

docs.title: Session 6 — Two-Button Logic Gates and a Shifting LED
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Read two push-buttons wired with internal pull-ups as digital inputs, use them to reproduce OR, AND and XOR logic on a single LED bus, and then use the same two buttons to shift one lit LED back and forth across four positions with wrap-around.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: GP10 → PIN_D, GP11 → PIN_C, GP12 → PIN_B, GP13 → PIN_A (same 4-LED bus as Session 4); GP16 → PIN_BA (button A), GP17 → PIN_BB (button B), both configured as inputs with gpio_pull_up().
  • PIN_BC (GP18) and PIN_BD (GP19) are also wired on the breadboard, but the code never reads them (no if checks either one) — they were meant for a third exercise that we didn't get to.
  • Non-default: buttons use the RP2350's internal pull-ups (no external resistor), so a press reads as a 0 (low), not a 1 — every button test in the code has to check for that low level.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Reused the 4-LED bus from Session 4 (GP10–GP13) and added two push-buttons on GP16 and GP17, each set as input with gpio_pull_up().
  2. Wrote three versions of the same program — identical setup, only the if condition on the two button states changes — to make the LED bus behave like an OR, an AND, and an XOR gate.
  3. Wrote a fourth program that uses the same two buttons to move a single lit LED across the four positions, one step per press, wrapping around at both ends.
  4. Recorded each behavior on video as evidence.

Shared setup code (identical in all four programs — only the loop body changes):

#define PIN_A 13
#define PIN_B 12
#define PIN_C 11
#define PIN_D 10

#define PIN_BA 16
#define PIN_BB 17
#define PIN_BC 18
#define PIN_BD 19

gpio_init(PIN_A);
gpio_init(PIN_B);
gpio_init(PIN_C);
gpio_init(PIN_D);

gpio_init(PIN_BA);
gpio_init(PIN_BB);
gpio_init(PIN_BC);
gpio_init(PIN_BD);

gpio_pull_up(PIN_BA);
gpio_pull_up(PIN_BB);
gpio_pull_up(PIN_BC);
gpio_pull_up(PIN_BD);

const uint32_t MASK =
    (1u << PIN_A) | (1u << PIN_B) | (1u << PIN_C) | (1u << PIN_D);
const uint32_t MASKB =
    (1u << PIN_BA) | (1u << PIN_BB) | (1u << PIN_BC) | (1u << PIN_BD);

// OE = Output Enable
sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK;
sio_hw->gpio_oe_clr = MASKB;

docs.title: Exercise 1 — OR gate
docs.text:
LED bus on if button A or button B is pressed (pull-up, so "pressed" means the bit reads 0 — hence the !).

while (true) {
    if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BA)) || !(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BB))) {
        sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK;
    } else {
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    sleep_ms(1);
}

docs.title: Exercise 2 — AND gate
docs.text:
LED bus on only when both buttons are pressed at the same time.

while (true) {
    if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BA)) && !(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BB))) {
        sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK;
    } else {
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    sleep_ms(1);
}

docs.title: Exercise 3 — XOR gate
docs.text:
LED bus on when exactly one of the two buttons is pressed; off if neither, and off again if both.

while (true) {
    if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BA)) && (sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BB))) {
        sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK;
    } else if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BB)) && (sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BA))) {
        sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK;
    } else {
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    sleep_ms(1);
}

docs.title: Exercise 4 — Shift the lit LED left/right
docs.text:
One button advances a counter (0–3) and the other decreases it; only the LED at position counter is lit; a flag makes each button press count once instead of repeating every 1 ms while held; the counter wraps at both edges of the 4-LED bus.

int counter = 0;
int flag = 0;

while (true) {
    sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u << (counter + 10));

    if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BA)) && (flag == 0)) {
        counter++;
        flag = 1;
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    else if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BB)) && (flag == 0)) {
        counter--;
        flag = 1;
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    else if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BB))) {
        // button B still held, already handled — wait for release
    }
    else if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u<<PIN_BA))) {
        // button A still held, already handled — wait for release
    }
    else {
        flag = 0;   // neither button pressed → re-arm for the next press
    }

    if (counter > 3) {
        counter = 0;
    } else if (counter < 0) {
        counter = 3;
    }
    sleep_ms(1);
}

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text: • The buttons use internal pull-ups, so a press reads as a 0, not a 1. I had seen this before and knew it in principle, but in the moment I blanked on it and spent a while testing different if conditions without getting anywhere, instead of stopping to work it out on paper. My professor noticed something was off and asked what was going on — that's when it clicked that I should have asked for help right away instead of losing time guessing alone. Going to review boolean/bitwise logic basics before the next session so this sticks.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text:
• In Exercise 4, the whole bus is cleared and one LED is re-set on every step. Session 4 used gpio_togl to flip only the bit that changes — could that replace the clear-then-set pattern here too, instead of turning all four LEDs off on every step?
  • Build the third exercise using PIN_BC / PIN_BD — didn't get to it this session.

docs.title: Session 8 — Interrupt-Driven LED Roulette (Speed Control + Center Stop)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Drive a 5-LED "roulette" light chaser from the SIO registers and control its speed, and its stop condition, with three push-button GPIO interrupts instead of polling.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: PIN_A=GP8, PIN_B=GP7, PIN_C=GP6, PIN_D=GP5, PIN_E=GP4 → 5 LEDs (with series resistors) forming the roulette; PIN_BA=GP16 (speed up / harder), PIN_BB=GP17 (slow down / easier), PIN_BC=GP18 (stop, only counts on the center LED).
  • Photo of the breadboard:
  • Non-default: internal pull-ups enabled on PIN_BA, PIN_BB, PIN_BC (gpio_pull_up), so all three buttons are active-low and the ISR fires on GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL. LEDs are driven directly through sio_hw (no gpio_put). Default 150 MHz clk_sys, nothing else changed.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired the 5 LEDs (with resistors) to GP4–GP8 and the 3 push buttons to GP16–GP18 with internal pull-ups.
  2. Wrote the chase loop with sio_hw->gpio_set / gpio_clr, bouncing counter from 0 up to 4 and back down so the lit LED sweeps E→A→E instead of just wrapping around.
  3. Registered the interrupt callback once, on PIN_BA, with gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback, then enabled PIN_BB and PIN_BC with plain gpio_set_irq_enabled (all three share the same ISR).
  4. Inside the ISR: PIN_BA decreases speed (floor 100 ms), PIN_BB increases it, and PIN_BC — only when counter == 2 — clears every LED and calls a blocking blink routine.
  5. Flashed the board, tested each button by hand, and recorded a short demo (audio removed): img/s08_roulette_demo.mp4.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: # File What it shows E1 img/s08_roulette_demo.mp4 Chase running at default speed (~0:00), then visibly faster after pressing the speed-up button a few times (~0:06–0:09) and then slower after pressing the speed-down button (~0:09-0:12) Confirms speed actually changes on a button press E2 img/s08_roulette_demo.mp4 Right near the end of the clip (~0:16.8 s), all 5 LEDs turn off together while the lit LED (the middle one) start to blink Confirms the winning condition

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Callback overwritten: I called gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback once per button (once for PIN_BA, once for PIN_BB, once for PIN_BC), assuming each call attached its own handler. It doesn't — that function sets one shared callback per core, so each new call silently replaced the previous one and only the last button actually worked. Fix: call gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback once (on PIN_BA) and use plain gpio_set_irq_enabled for PIN_BB and PIN_BC, since all three land in the same gpio_isr anyway.
  • static instead of volatile: speed and counter were first declared static. The main loop kept reading a stale value because the compiler had no reason to think the ISR could change them between reads. Switching both to volatile fixed it.
  • sleep_ms inside the ISR: the first version of the "stop" blink called sleep_ms() from inside gpio_isr, which froze the whole program — sleep_ms waits on the timer/event system, and calling it from interrupt context stalled everything instead of just pausing. Replaced it with busy_wait_ms inside blink_blocking, so the ISR blocks the CPU on purpose without touching the timer/event hardware.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
...
volatile int speed = 500;   // was `static` — main loop read a stale copy
volatile int counter = 0;
...

static void gpio_isr(uint gpio, uint32_t events) {
    if (events & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL) {
        if (gpio == PIN_BC && counter == 2) {          // only stop on the center LED
            ...
            blink_blocking(6, 50, 300);              // busy_wait_ms inside — see below
        } else if (gpio == PIN_BB) {
            speed = speed + 50;                      // slow down
        } else if (gpio == PIN_BA) {
            if (speed >= 100) speed = speed - 50;    // speed up, floor at 100 ms
        }
    }
    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}

...

int main(void) {
    ...
    // register the callback ONCE — a second call with a different pin overwrites it
    gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(PIN_BA, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true, &gpio_isr);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(PIN_BB, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);   // shares the same ISR
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(PIN_BC, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    ...
}

Full file at src/s08_roulette/Roulette.c.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: Why does a second gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback call silently replace the first instead of raising an error — is there really only one raw NVIC entry point per core for every GPIO pin, with the SDK keeping a single function-pointer slot that all pins' edge events get dispatched through? Want to check irq.c in the Pico SDK next session to see how the shared handler figures out which pin actually fired.

docs.title: Timers — Repeating Timer on GP15 (Predict vs Measure)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Generate a square wave on GP15 from an SDK repeating timer (no sleep_ms in the loop), predict its period, frequency and duty cycle from TOGGLE_MS, and check the prediction on the oscilloscope.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
The callback toggles GP15 once every TOGGLE_MS, so one full period is one HIGH plus one LOW:

  • T = 2 · TOGGLE_MS f = 1 / T = 1000 / (2 · TOGGLE_MS) Hz duty = 50 % (HIGH and LOW both last TOGGLE_MS)
  • TOGGLE_MS = 250 → HIGH = LOW = 250 ms, T = 500 ms, f = 1000 / 500 = 2.000 Hz
  • TOGGLE_MS = 10 → HIGH = LOW = 10 ms, T = 20 ms, f = 1000 / 20 = 50.00 Hz

With a negative delay (-TOGGLE_MS) the callbacks are scheduled start-to-start, so I expected no drift: at most a few µs of jitter from interrupt latency on each edge.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: GP15 → scope CH1 (timer output); scope ground → a Pico GND pin only. GP14 (CH2 callback marker) was not used in these captures.
  • Photo of the breadboard: not taken this session (only the Pico and the probe on GP15 / GND).
  • Non-default: none. Default 150 MHz clk_sys, timer at its default 1 µs tick, no pulls, no external parts. Scope at 5 kS/s, 10k points, trigger on CH1 rising edge.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Copied the course repeating-timer code, set OUT_PIN = 15, TOGGLE_MS = 250, add_repeating_timer_ms(-TOGGLE_MS, …).
  2. Built and flashed; probed GP15 on CH1, 200 ms/div, added Frequency / Period / +Width / −Width measurements → E1.
  3. Changed only TOGGLE_MS to 10, rebuilt and flashed.
  4. Zoomed in 50× (4 ms/div) on the 200 ms/div record → E2.
  5. Saved a second capture 3 s later to check repeatability → E3.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• "Too perfect" readings — we couldn't see any delay: we expected something like 500.12 ms or 501 ms (callback/interrupt overhead adding up), but E1 reads exactly 500.0 ms and E2 exactly 20.00 ms. At first we thought the scope was "correcting" the value. What we found by looking at the numbers again:
    • The readout has only 4 digits: at 500.0 ms the smallest step is 100 µs, and at 20.00 ms it is 10 µs. Anything smaller is rounded away.
    • The sampling is 5 kS/s → 200 µs between samples (see the 5.00 kS/s field annotated in E2), so a few µs of shift on an edge cannot be resolved visually.
    • The actual error is tiny: with -TOGGLE_MS each deadline is previous deadline + TOGGLE_MS, so the ISR latency (a few µs at 150 MHz) causes jitter, not drift — it doesn't accumulate. The only place it shows is the Std Dev column: σ(T) ≈ 1.9 µs in E2/E3.
    • Fix / how to see it next time: use a faster timebase (e.g. 1–10 µs/div around one edge, ≥ 1 MS/s) and read Std Dev or Min/Max instead of the Value column.
  • Polluted statistics in E1: the Mean/Min/Max columns in E1 show impossible values (Min period 2.4 ms, Max frequency 416.7 Hz, Mean 14.55 Hz) for a 2 Hz signal. Those come from samples taken before the signal was stable (probe being connected / previous program), and the statistics were never reset. We trusted only the Value column for E1; next time press Reset Statistics after the signal settles.

#define TOGGLE_MS  250          // only line changed between runs (250 → 10)

static bool toggle_cb(repeating_timer_t *t) {
    level = !level;
    gpio_put(OUT_PIN, level);   // short callback, no sleeps
    return true;                // keep repeating
}

int main(void) {
    ...
    repeating_timer_t timer;

    while (true) tight_loop_contents();   // main() is free

docs.title: PWM — LED Fade, Clock Divider and an 8-Key Piano (Predict vs Measure)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Predict a PWM signal's frequency and duty from clk_sys, the clock divider and TOP and check it on the oscilloscope (Part 1, LED), then use the same formula backwards to play notes on a speaker with an 8-key PWM piano (Part 2).

docs.title: Part 1 — LED Fade, Clock Divider and Fixed Duty
Prediction
docs.text:
A PWM slice counts 0 … TOP at clk_sys / div, so:

  • f_PWM = f_clk / (div · (TOP + 1)) duty = level / (TOP + 1) +W = duty · T
  • Course example (F_PWM_HZ = 2000, TOP = 1023, f_clk = 150 MHz): div = 150 MHz / (2000 · 1024) = 73.24 → f = 2.000 kHz, T = 500.0 µs
  • DIV_10 (div = 10, TOP = 4095): 150 MHz / (10 · 4096) → f = 3.662 kHz, T = 273.1 µs
  • DIV_1 (div = 1, TOP = 4095): 150 MHz / (1 · 4096) → f = 36.62 kHz, T = 27.31 µs
  • Fixed duty at 2 kHz, TOP = 1023: 35 % → +W ≈ 175 µs, 87 % → +W ≈ 435 µs, 20 % → +W ≈ 100 µs
  • Fade (step = 8, sleep_ms(5)): the level sweeps 0 → TOP → 0 like a triangle, so a random scope snapshot sees a roughly uniform duty between 0 and 100 %: mean ≈ 50 %, σ ≈ 100 / √12 = 28.9 %. Ramp time ≈ (TOP / 8) · 5 ms = 0.64 s for TOP = 1023 (2.56 s for TOP = 4095).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: LED_PIN = GP2 → LED (with series resistor) and scope CH1; scope ground → a Pico GND pin.
  • Photo of the breadboard: not taken this session (Pico 2 W, one LED on GP2, probe on GP2 / GND).
  • Non-default: none. Default 150 MHz clk_sys. Scope at 5 MS/s (200 µs/div) for the 2 kHz runs, 10 MS/s and 100 MS/s for the faster ones; 10k points, trigger on CH1 rising edge at 920 mV.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Flashed the course pwm_led.c (fade, 2 kHz, TOP = 1023) and probed GP2 at 200 µs/div with Frequency / Period / +Width / Duty measurements → E1–E3.
  2. Did the divider math by hand with a calculator and left it as an integer (div = 73 instead of 73.24), reflashed and measured again → E2, E3.
  3. Changed TOP to 4095 and set the divider to 10 (DIV_10), then to 1 (DIV_1), keeping the fade → E4, E5.
  4. Went back to 2 kHz (TOP = 1023, div = 73), turned the fade off and wrote a fixed level for 35 %, 87 % and 20 % duty → E6–E8.
  5. Compared every Value/Mean reading with the formula above.

Conclusion: f = f_clk / (div · (TOP + 1)) predicted every frequency to within the divider's fractional resolution, and duty = level / (TOP + 1) gave the fixed duties to within one scope sample. Lowering the divider ×10 multiplies the frequency ×10 (E4 → E5) without changing the duty behavior; TOP trades frequency for resolution.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• 2.002 / 2.007 kHz instead of 2.000 kHz: the prediction said exactly 2 kHz, but E1 reads 2.002 kHz and the later runs 2.006–2.007 kHz. Two causes, both in the divider:
    • With the course float (E1): the RP2350 stores the divider as 8 integer + 4 fractional bits (steps of 1/16), and pwm_set_clkdiv() truncates the float, so 73.24 becomes 73.1875 → 2001.5 Hz.
    • With our calculator value (E2–E8): we did the math by hand and left the divider as the integer 73, dropping the 0.24 → 150 MHz / (73 · 1024) = 2006.6 Hz, i.e. +0.33 %. The scope matched the divider we actually wrote, not the 2 kHz we wanted.
    • Fix: pick TOP and div so the divider is exact — e.g. TOP = 999, div = 75 → 150 MHz / (75 · 1000) = exactly 2000 Hz — or compute the real frequency from the stored divider instead of the requested one.
  • Polluted statistics: E2/E3 show Min period = 350 ns and Max frequency = 2.857 MHz, which are impossible for a 2 kHz PWM. They came from glitches while reflashing / reconnecting the probe, and the statistics were never reset. We trusted only the Value and Mean columns; next time press Reset Statistics after the signal settles.
  • "Value" duty means nothing during the fade: E1–E5 show duties of 17 %, 60 %, 79 %, 95 %… depending on when the snapshot was taken. For the fade, the useful numbers are Mean (≈ 50 %) and Std Dev (≈ 28.9 %), not Value.

docs.title: Divider per note
docs.text:
Same formula as Part 1, solved for the divider: div = f_clk / (f_note · (TOP + 1)), with f_clk = clock_get_hz(clk_sys) = 150 MHz and TOP = 1023. The hardware keeps the divider in steps of 1/16, so the note that comes out is 150 MHz / (⌊16·div⌋/16 · 1024):

docs.text:
• Pin map: GP2 (BUZZER_PIN) → series resistor → speaker (+), speaker (−) → GND; GP3–GP10 → 8 note buttons (C6 … C7); GP11 → BTN_UP, GP12 → BTN_DOWN (level ± 64).
  • Photo of the breadboard:
  • Non-default: internal pull-ups on GP3–GP12 (gpio_pull_up), so every button is active-low; buttons read straight from sio_hw->gpio_in. The divider is a float computed from clock_get_hz(clk_sys), not an integer typed in by hand.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired 8 note buttons on GP3–GP10, two level buttons on GP11/GP12, and the speaker through a resistor on GP2.
  2. Wrote piano.c: TOP = 1023 fixed, a table NOTAS[8], and in the loop the first pressed key sets pwm_set_clkdiv(slice, f_clk / (NOTAS[i] · 1024)) and enables the slice; no key → slice disabled (silence).
  3. Added BTN_UP / BTN_DOWN to move the channel level in steps of 64 (6.25 % duty), clamped to 0 … TOP.
  4. Flashed it, played a few melodies across all 8 keys and recorded it with sound: img/pwm_piano_demo.mp4.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• One key at a time: pressing two keys plays only the lower one, because the for loop breaks on the first pressed key and a slice can only produce one frequency. A chord would need a second slice/pin.
  • sleep_ms(150) in the volume buttons blocks the keys: while BTN_UP/BTN_DOWN is held, the loop only runs every ~155 ms, so the note keys respond late. It's acceptable for a demo; a timer/IRQ-based debounce (like Session 8) would fix it.
  • The "volume" buttons don't really change volume linearly: they change the duty. The loudest fundamental is at 50 % (level = 512); moving up or down from there makes the tone quieter and thinner, and at 0 % or 100 % (level 0 / TOP) there is no sound at all.

docs.title: Code (piano)
docs.text:
#define TOP 1023
const uint32_t NOTAS[8] = {1046, 1175, 1318, 1397, 1568, 1760, 1975, 2093};

float f_clk = (float)clock_get_hz(clk_sys);        // 150 MHz, not hard-coded
pwm_set_wrap(slice, TOP);
int level = (TOP + 1) / 2;                          // 50 % = strongest fundamental

for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
    if ((sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u << (BTN_BASE + i))) == 0) {        // active-low key
        float div = f_clk / ((float)NOTAS[i] * (float)(TOP + 1)); // keep the fraction!
        pwm_set_clkdiv(slice, div);
        pwm_set_enabled(slice, true);
        note_pressed = true;
        break;                                       // one note at a time
    }
}
if (!note_pressed) pwm_set_enabled(slice, false);   // silence

docs.title: ADC — LDR, Electret Noise Detector, Potentiometer Angle and NTC Temperature
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Read analog sensors with the RP2350 ADC: an LDR (EMA-filtered, converted to volts and a 0–100 % light level) and an electret microphone (fixed-threshold noise detector) on ADC0, plus a potentiometer (ADC1 → 0–270°) and an NTC thermistor (ADC0 → °C with the Beta equation) read together by switching channels.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: LDR_GPIO_PIN = GP26 → LDR_ADC_INPUT = ADC0. The same pin/channel is used for the electret (one sensor at a time, separate programs).
  • LDR: voltage divider between 3.3 V and GND, midpoint to GP26. The reading goes up with light, so the LDR is on the 3.3 V side and the fixed resistor on the GND side.
  • Electret: electret capsule with its bias resistor, a coupling capacitor and a resistor divider that centers the signal around mid-supply before GP26.
  • Potentiometer + NTC (Wokwi simulation): potentiometer wiper → GP27 (ADC1), NTC temperature module (analog out) → GP26 (ADC0), both powered from 3.3 V / GND of the Pico 2. The temperature is set with the sensor's slider in the simulator.
  • Non-default: none. adc_gpio_init(26) disables the digital input buffer and pulls on the pin; ADC in free single-shot mode (adc_read()), default 150 MHz clk_sys. USB serial monitor at 115200 baud.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Initialized the ADC (adc_init, adc_gpio_init(26), adc_select_input(0)) and printed raw values to find the dark/bright extremes of the LDR → used them as LDR_MIN = 9 and LDR_MAX = 3600.
  2. Added the EMA filter from the course notes (α = 0.0625), seeded with the first sample so it doesn't start from 0.
  3. Converted the filtered value to volts and to a percentage, and printed Raw | Filtro | Voltaje | Nivel every 100 ms.
  4. Recorded a demo: hands covering the LDR, then uncovered (room light), then a phone flashlight on top and moving away → img/adc_ldr_demo.mp4 (audio removed).
  5. Swapped the LDR for the electret front end and flashed adcmicrosencillo.c, which prints the raw value every 100 ms and labels it "Ruido alto" when raw > 2110, otherwise "Ruido normal".
  6. Wrote pot_temp.c in Wokwi: each loop selects ADC1 (pot) and then ADC0 (NTC) with adc_select_input, applies a separate EMA to each, maps the pot to grados = ema · 270 / 4095, and converts the NTC reading to °C with the Beta equation (β = 3950, T0 = 25 °C). Loop every 10 ms.
  7. Moved the NTC slider (18.8 → 80 → −24 °C) and turned the pot across its range while recording the serial output → img/adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Wiring error on the temperature sensor: we made a mistake when connecting the temperature sensor, so it did not give a valid reading at first and we had to recheck the wiring before it worked.
  • No instrumented electret, so only a simple noise detector: we didn't buy the electret module with its own amplifier, so we only had the bare capsule with a basic bias/divider front end. Its signal is small, so instead of actually measuring sound level we built a simple noise detector: one raw sample compared against a fixed threshold (2110, ≈ 1.70 V) that prints "Ruido alto" / "Ruido normal".
  • Calibrating the potentiometer reading took some effort: getting the potentiometer measurement to map correctly to its full range took several tries until the raw range 0–4095 matched the actual value of the potentiometer.

// LDR — EMA filter + conversion (Fotorresistencia.c)
uint16_t x = adc_read();                       // 0..4095
if (!y_init) { y = (float)x; y_init = true; }  // seed with first sample
else          y = alpha * (float)x + (1.0f - alpha) * y;   // alpha = 1/16

uint16_t y_u16 = (uint16_t)(y + 0.5f);
float voltaje  = (y_u16 * 3.3f) / 4095.0f;
int porcentaje = ((y_u16 - LDR_MIN) * 100) / (LDR_MAX - LDR_MIN);

// Electret — fixed threshold (adcmicrosencillo.c)

if (m > 2110) printf("Raw=%u | Ruido alto\n", m);    // ~1.70 V, ~62 LSB above mid-scale
else          printf("Raw=%u | Ruido normal\n", m);
sleep_ms(100);

// Potentiometer + NTC — two channels in the same loop (pot_temp.c)
adc_select_input(Pot_INPUT);                  // ADC1 -> GP27
uint16_t xp = adc_read();
p = alpha * (float)xp + (1.0f - alpha) * p;
uint16_t grados = (uint16_t)(p + 0.5f) * 270 / 4095;

adc_select_input(Temp_INPUT);                 // ADC0 -> GP26
uint16_t xt = adc_read();
t = alpha * (float)xt + (1.0f - alpha) * t;
double a = (double)(uint16_t)(t + 0.5f);
float temperatura = (float)(1.0 / (log(1.0 / (4095.0 / a - 1.0)) / BETA
                    + 1.0 / 298.15) - 273.15);  // Beta equation, T0 = 25 °C

docs.text: For the electret, a single sample every 100 ms can't really "hear" anything. Next session I want to sample fast (e.g. ~8–10 kHz with a tight loop or the ADC FIFO / free-running mode), compute the peak-to-peak or RMS over a 100 ms window around the 2048 bias, and compare that against a threshold. I'd also like to check the actual bias point of my front end — if it's not close to 2048, a fixed 2110 threshold could be almost always "alto" or never "alto" depending on the resistors.

docs.title: I2C — Reading a DS1307 RTC and an MPU6050 on the Same Bus (Wokwi)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Use i2c0 of the Pico 2 as a master to read the time/date from a DS1307 RTC and the accelerometer, gyroscope and temperature from an MPU6050 — two slaves sharing the same SDA/SCL lines — using the write register pointer + repeated START + read sequence, and print the decoded values over USB serial.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: SDA_PIN=GP4 (I2C0 SDA), SCL_PIN=GP5 (I2C0 SCL), both shared by the two slaves. DS1307 RTC at 0x68, MPU6050 at 0x69 (its AD0 pin tied high). Both modules powered from the Pico's 3V3 and GND.
  • Screenshot of the Wokwi circuit:
  • Non-default: simulated in Wokwi (no physical board). i2c0 at 100 kHz (standard mode). Internal pull-ups enabled on SDA and SCL (gpio_pull_up) instead of external resistors. MPU6050 left at its default ranges: ±2 g (16384 LSB/g) and ±250 °/s (131 LSB/(°/s)). Default 150 MHz clk_sys, nothing else changed.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Placed the Pico 2, a DS1307 and an MPU6050 in Wokwi and wired both modules to the same SDA (GP4) / SCL (GP5) lines; tied the MPU6050's AD0 to VCC so it answers at 0x69 instead of 0x68.
  2. Initialized i2c0 at 100 kHz, set GP4/GP5 to GPIO_FUNC_I2C and enabled their pull-ups.
  3. RTC: i2c_write_blocking of register 0x00 with nostop=true, then i2c_read_blocking of 7 bytes (repeated START) → printed HH:MM:SS and DD/MM/YY directly in hex, since the DS1307 stores them in BCD.
  4. MPU6050: same sequence starting at register 0x3B (ACCEL_XOUT_H) and reading 14 bytes; rebuilt each int16_t as (high << 8) | low and converted to g, °/s and °C (temp/340 + 36.53).
  5. Ran the simulation, moved the MPU6050 sliders and recorded the screen (audio removed): img/i2c_wokwi_demo.mp4.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: # File What it shows E1 img/i2c_wokwi_demo.mp4 ~0:03 → ~0:09: the RTC lines go from 19:04:59 to 19:05:05 with date 09/11/26, printing every 2 s (1 s after the RTC read + 1 s after the MPU read) The 7-byte read from 0x68 works and the BCD can be printed straight as %02X E2 img/i2c_wokwi_demo.mp4 ~0:00–0:04: sliders at Y = −1.4 g, gyro Y = 152 °/s, Z = 19 °/s, 52.2 °C → terminal prints Y: -1.40, Y: 152.00, Z: 19.00, 52.2 °C The 14-byte burst from 0x69 and the conversion formulas are correct E3 img/i2c_wokwi_demo.mp4 ~0:09–0:14: after moving the sliders to Y = 1.75 g, Z = −1.65 g, gyro Y = −170 °/s, Z = 181 °/s, −14.2 °C, the next print shows exactly those values (signs included) Negative values survive the int16_t cast, and both slaves keep answering on the same bus

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Two slaves at the same address: the DS1307 has a fixed address of 0x68, and the MPU6050's default address is also 0x68 (AD0 = 0). With both on the bus at 0x68, a read can't tell which device is answering. Fix: tie the MPU6050's AD0 pin high, which moves it to 0x69, and use MPU_ADDR 0x69 in the code.
  • Copy-paste in the MPU error branches: the MPU block was copied from the RTC block, and its error printfs still printed w and r (the RTC's return values) instead of w2 and r2. It never showed up in the demo because both devices always ACK in Wokwi, but if the MPU failed, the message would report the RTC's result and hide the real error code. Fix: use w2 / r2 in those printfs (corrected in src/i2c/i2c.c).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
#define RTC_ADDR 0x68   // DS1307 (fixed)
#define MPU_ADDR 0x69   // MPU6050 with AD0 = 1, so it doesn't collide with the RTC
...
// START + addr|W + reg 0x3B, no STOP → REPEATED START + addr|R + 14 bytes + NACK + STOP
int w2 = i2c_write_blocking(I2C_PORT, MPU_ADDR, &regmpu, 1, /*nostop=*/true);
if (w2 < 0) { printf("I2C error (ret=%d)\n", w2); goto next2; }   // was `w`
int r2 = i2c_read_blocking(I2C_PORT, MPU_ADDR, memory2, sizeof(memory2), /*nostop=*/false);
...
int16_t accel_y_raw = (memory2[2] << 8) | memory2[3];   // big-endian: high byte first
int16_t temp_raw    = (memory2[6] << 8) | memory2[7];
float accel_y     = accel_y_raw / 16384.0;              // ±2 g
float temperatura = (temp_raw / 340.0) + 36.53;         // datasheet formula
...
// RTC registers are BCD, so %02X prints them as decimal digits
printf("%02X:%02X:%02X \n", memory[2], memory[1], memory[0]);

Full file at src/i2c/i2c.c.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: On a real MPU6050, register PWR_MGMT_1 (0x6B) powers up with the SLEEP bit set, so reading 0x3B without first writing 0x00 to 0x6B should return all zeros — yet in Wokwi the values came out correct without that write. Next time I want to try it on real hardware to see whether the wake-up write is needed, and also print the raw memory[0] of the DS1307 to check the CH (clock halt) bit 7, which my %02X print of the seconds would show as 80+ if the oscillator were stopped.

docs.title: UART — Two-Pico Button/LED Mirror
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Connect two Pico 2 boards through UART0 so that pressing a button on one board turns on the matching LED on the other board, and releasing it turns that LED off — in both directions, with the same firmware on both boards.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map (identical on both boards): TX_PIN=GP0 (UART0 TX), RX_PIN=GP1 (UART0 RX); Button_A=GP12, Button_B=GP13, Button_C=GP14; Led_A=GP16, Led_B=GP17, Led_C=GP18 (each LED with its series resistor).
  • Board-to-board wiring: GP0 (TX) of board 1 → GP1 (RX) of board 2, GP0 (TX) of board 2 → GP1 (RX) of board 1, and a shared GND between both breadboards.
  • Photo of the setup:
  • Non-default: internal pull-ups on the three buttons (gpio_pull_up), so a press reads 0. UART0 configured as 115200 baud, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity (uart_set_format(UART_ID, 8, 1, UART_PARITY_NONE)). Default 150 MHz clk_sys, nothing else changed.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired 3 buttons (GP12–GP14) and 3 LEDs (GP16–GP18) on each breadboard, then crossed TX/RX between the two Picos and joined their grounds.
  2. Configured GP0/GP1 as GPIO_FUNC_UART and initialized uart0 at 115200 8N1.
  3. Defined a tiny protocol of one character per event: uppercase ('A', 'B', 'C') = button pressed → LED on; lowercase ('a', 'b', 'c') = button released → LED off.
  4. Used one flag per button so each letter is sent only once per press/release edge, and on the receive side read every byte available with while (uart_is_readable(...)), acting only on those six letters.
  5. Flashed the same program to both boards, tested every button in both directions and recorded a short demo (audio removed): img/uart_demo.mp4.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: # File What it shows E1 img/uart_demo.mp4 ~0:01–0:04: a button is pressed on the bottom board and the LED on the top board turns on while the button is held Board 2 → Board 1 direction works E2 img/uart_demo.mp4 ~0:05–0:09: a button is pressed on the top board and the matching LED on the bottom board turns on, then turns off on release Board 1 → Board 2 direction works, and the release (lowercase letter) turns it off

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Letters sent over and over: the first version did if (gpio_get(Button_A) == 0) uart_putc(UART_ID, 'A'); inside the loop, so as long as the button was held it kept sending 'A' every 10 ms — the other board received a continuous stream instead of one event. Fix: add flag_a / flag_b / flag_c so the letter is sent only on the edge (when the button goes from released to pressed) and a lowercase letter only when it goes back.
  • LEDs turning off by themselves (else on the receiver): in that first version I only sent uppercase letters to turn LEDs on, and the receiver did if (c == 'A') gpio_put(Led_A, 1); else gpio_put(Led_A, 0);. On the terminal it looked like only my letters were arriving, but there were "gaps" where something else was received that didn't show (non-printable characters such as \r/\n, or simply the letter of a different button). Any byte that wasn't 'A' fell into the else and turned LED A off, even though I was still holding the button. Fix: send an explicit off command ('a', 'b', 'c') on release and remove the generic else — now each LED only changes when its own two letters arrive, and any other byte is ignored.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
// --- SEND: only on edges (flag), not every loop iteration ---
if (gpio_get(Button_A) == 0 && flag_a == 0) {
    uart_putc(UART_ID, 'A');      // pressed
    flag_a = 1;
} else if (gpio_get(Button_A) == 1 && flag_a == 1) {
    uart_putc(UART_ID, 'a');      // released
    flag_a = 0;
}
...
// --- RECEIVE: only react to our own letters, no generic else ---
while (uart_is_readable(UART_ID)) {
    char c = uart_getc(UART_ID);
    if (c == 'A')      gpio_put(Led_A, 1);
    else if (c == 'a') gpio_put(Led_A, 0);   // any other byte is ignored
    ...
}
sleep_ms(10);

Full file at src/uart/uart.c.

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: The receiver uses polling with sleep_ms(10) between checks. At 115200 baud one character takes ~87 µs, so in those 10 ms about 115 characters could arrive, but the RX FIFO only holds 16. With three buttons sending single letters this shouldn't fill up, but if the other board sent a burst (for example a full text string) bytes would be lost to an overrun. Next session I want to switch the receive side to the UART RX interrupt with a circular buffer (as in the course example) and check the OE (overrun) flag in the RSR register to see whether polling actually drops anything.

docs.title: 🚀 Comandos básicos de Git (primeros pasos)
docs.text: En este curso solo usaremos los comandos esenciales de Git para trabajar con repositorios.

docs.title: 1. Clonar un repositorio
docs.text:
Copia un proyecto de GitHub a tu computadora.

git clone https://github.com/usuario/repositorio.git

docs.title: 2. Verificar cambios
docs.text:
Muestra qué archivos has modificado o agregado.

git status

docs.title: 3. Preparar cambios
docs.text:
Agrega archivos para guardarlos en el próximo commit.

git add archivo.txt
git add .   # agrega todos los archivos modificados

docs.title: 4. Guardar cambios (commit)
docs.text:
Guarda tus cambios con un mensaje descriptivo.

git commit -m "Descripción breve de los cambios"

docs.title: 5. Subir cambios al repositorio (push)
docs.text:
Envía tus commits locales al repositorio en GitHub.

git push origin main

docs.title: 6. Traer cambios del remoto (pull)
docs.text:
Actualiza tu proyecto con los últimos cambios de GitHub.

git pull origin main

docs.title: Flujo típico de trabajo
docs.text:
1. Traer cambios del remoto 

    git pull origin main

  2. Editar tus archivos de proyecto.

  3. Preparar los cambios 

    git add .

  4. Guardar los cambios 

    git commit -m "Mensaje descriptivo"

  5. Enviar los cambios al remoto 

    git push origin main

Consejo

Piensa en este ciclo como un loop infinito: cada vez que quieras contribuir → primero pull, después add + commit, y finalmente push.
